items.prompt: Distinguish between public-sector and private-sector organisation. A fictional municipal workshop, Ombili Services, is controlled by its local authority; nearby Ekuva Repairs is controlled by its individual owner. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Public and private sectors classify activity by ownership and control. A public-sector enterprise is owned and controlled by the state, whereas private-sector activity is owned and controlled by private individuals or organisations. A government-owned bus operator and an individually owned bus operator can provide the same service while belonging to different ownership sectors. Their activity does not settle their ownership. A mixed economy combines public and private activity. Public provision can pursue access to essential services or employment as well as financial sustainability. Private owners commonly seek profit and business survival, although a private organisation may also pursue social aims. Neither label proves that the organisation is efficient or that every service is free. Public enterprises may charge customers and private providers may supply services under government contracts. Organising privately can involve a sole trader, partnership or company; public activity can be organised through government departments or state-owned enterprises. Ownership forms are developed in topic 2.1. A company described as public limited has shares available to the public; that name does not by itself make it state owned. Ask who owns and controls it before assigning its ownership sector. Both repair vehicles, but Ombili is public sector and Ekuva is private sector. Charging a repair fee does not change Ombili’s owner, and serving government vehicles does not make Ekuva a public enterprise.
marking_guidance: Difference: Public and private sectors classify activity by ownership and control.

items.prompt: Define public sector. [2]
items.canonical_answer: The public sector comprises organisations owned and controlled by the state. State ownership, rather than whether the public uses a service, is the defining feature. Public provision may aim to extend access to essential services, while still needing to manage costs and finance its operations. A public enterprise may sell its output; charging customers does not turn state ownership into private ownership.
marking_guidance: Meaning: The public sector comprises organisations owned and controlled by the state.

items.prompt: Define private sector. [2]
items.canonical_answer: The private sector comprises activity owned and controlled by private individuals or organisations rather than the state. It includes individually owned businesses and companies, and can include organisations with social aims. Supplying a government customer does not by itself transfer ownership to government. A private company can grow very large while remaining private sector.
marking_guidance: Meaning: The private sector comprises activity owned and controlled by private individuals or organisations rather than the state.

items.prompt: Distinguish between nationalisation and privatisation. Assume a fictional state-owned coach company is sold entirely to private investors. In a separate event the state buys a privately owned water supplier. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Nationalisation transfers a privately owned business or industry into state ownership and control. Privatisation transfers a state-owned business or activity into private ownership and control. The directions are opposite: private to state, or state to private. A new owner may change objectives, investment and decisions, but a change in owner is distinct from a guaranteed improvement in performance. Nationalisation may protect essential service access but creates state financing demands. Privatisation may introduce commercial incentives, but service conditions may be needed to protect unprofitable users. A sale to investors within Namibia is still privatisation if state ownership transfers to private owners. Nationalisation does not mean selling abroad or banning imports; those concern international trade, not a transfer of ownership. Identify the enterprise whose ownership changes. The coach sale is privatisation because ownership moves from state to private investors. The water purchase is nationalisation because it moves in the reverse direction. The buyers’ nationality does not determine either classification.
marking_guidance: Difference: Nationalisation transfers a privately owned business or industry into state ownership and control.

items.prompt: Distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary activities in a supply chain. Osha Clay extracts clay near Otjiwarongo, Imba Pots shapes and fires it, and Hela Couriers delivers the pots to buyers. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Activity sectors classify what is done. Primary businesses obtain natural resources; secondary businesses transform materials into products or carry out construction; tertiary businesses supply services. Follow the activity rather than the owner or product’s final user. Growing mahangu is primary, milling it into flour is secondary, and transporting or selling the flour is tertiary. Transport does not physically manufacture the flour even though it adds value by making it available where needed. A business can operate in more than one activity sector. An enterprise growing fruit, making juice and running its own shop has primary, secondary and tertiary operations. If asked to classify one operation, classify that operation. If describing the whole enterprise, explain its combination rather than assuming a single label covers every stage. Public/private ownership is a separate axis: a privately owned farm is both private sector and primary sector. Development of services does not remove the economy’s need for materials or manufactured goods; the sectors supply inputs and customers to one another. Extraction is primary; changing clay into pots is secondary; delivery is tertiary. A privately owned courier remains tertiary even if a public school buys its service. Classifying the process avoids confusing a customer’s ownership with a supplier’s activity.
marking_guidance: Difference: Activity sectors classify what is done.
Context: credit the specific case link or contrast stated in the answer; a copied name alone is insufficient.
Effect: credit the developed explanation or correctly executed working, rather than a repeated assertion.

items.prompt: Define primary sector. [2]
items.canonical_answer: The primary sector obtains natural resources from the land or sea. Farming, fishing, forestry and mineral extraction are examples. The classification concerns extraction or harvesting, before manufacturing transforms the resource into another product. Selling what a farm grows does not make the growing activity tertiary.
marking_guidance: Meaning: The primary sector obtains natural resources from the land or sea.

items.prompt: Define secondary sector. [2]
items.canonical_answer: The secondary sector transforms materials into manufactured products and includes construction. It takes inputs such as timber, flour or metal and changes them into an output such as a desk, loaf or gate. Being secondary does not mean less important; the term identifies the stage of activity. Delivery of a finished product is a separate service activity.
marking_guidance: Meaning: The secondary sector transforms materials into manufactured products and includes construction.

items.prompt: Define tertiary sector. [2]
items.canonical_answer: The tertiary sector provides services to consumers or other businesses. Retailing, transport, banking and repair services are examples. A service may support physical goods without manufacturing them: a carrier moves an existing product and a shop makes it available to buyers. A business’s classification follows its service activity rather than whether its customer is public or private.
marking_guidance: Meaning: The tertiary sector provides services to consumers or other businesses.

items.prompt: State two methods of measuring business size. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Business size can be described through legal form of ownership, nature of business, nature of product, capital employed, total assets, number of employees, level of technology, market share, turnover, profitability and value of output. Two straightforward numerical measures are the number of employees and annual turnover. No single indicator ranks every business fairly. A highly automated producer may employ fewer people than a labour-intensive workshop but produce much more. Some indicators are descriptive clues, such as ownership form or technology, rather than a numerical scale. Others measure different things: turnover is sales revenue, profit is the surplus after costs, and total assets is the value of resources owned. Select a measure suited to the comparison and state the time period or valuation basis. Compare similar activities where possible and use several indicators if they disagree. Large does not necessarily mean successful, profitable or well managed. A small specialist may earn a high profit relative to its investment, while a large producer can make a loss.
marking_guidance: Point: Business size can be described through legal form of ownership, nature of business, nature of product, capital employed, total assets, number of employees, level of technology, market share, turnover, profitability and value of output.

items.prompt: State two points about legal form as a size indicator: one use and one limitation. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Legal form identifies how a business is owned and organised, such as a sole trader, partnership or company. It is a descriptive clue to size because some company forms may make larger funding possible. Its limitation is that the form does not specify actual sales, employees or assets: a company can be small and a long-established individually owned business can be substantial.
marking_guidance: Point: Legal form identifies how a business is owned and organised, such as a sole trader, partnership or company.

items.prompt: State two ways in which business activity affects the interpretation of size comparisons. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Nature of business identifies the activity undertaken, such as mining, retailing or personal services. It helps choose meaningful size comparisons: mining often needs extensive equipment, while a personal service may depend mainly on labour. Its limitation is that activity is a category, not a measured quantity. A retailer is not automatically larger or smaller than a manufacturer.
marking_guidance: Point: Nature of business identifies the activity undertaken, such as mining, retailing or personal services.

items.prompt: State two reasons to examine the product supplied before comparing business scale. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Nature of product describes what is supplied and its characteristics, such as a low-priced standard item or a high-value customised item. It helps explain why units of output can be misleading. Its limitation is that the kind or price of product does not alone establish the business’s total scale. One expensive item and many inexpensive items require a comparable monetary measure.
marking_guidance: Point: Nature of product describes what is supplied and its characteristics, such as a low-priced standard item or a high-value customised item.

items.prompt: State two points about capital employed as a size measure: one use and one limitation. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Capital employed is the long-term finance used in a business, commonly measured as owners’ capital plus non-current liabilities, or total assets less current liabilities. A larger amount can indicate a greater scale of resources committed. Its limitation is that capital-intensive and labour-intensive activities need different investment, so it does not translate directly into jobs or sales. Use a consistent accounting basis.
marking_guidance: Point: Capital employed is the long-term finance used in a business, commonly measured as owners’ capital plus non-current liabilities, or total assets less current liabilities.

items.prompt: State two points about total assets as a size measure: one use and one limitation. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Total assets is the recorded value of all assets controlled by the business, including non-current and current assets. It indicates the resource base used to operate. Its limitation is that valuation dates and methods, the age of equipment and renting rather than owning premises can distort comparisons. A business with expensive assets may use them poorly or sell little output.
marking_guidance: Point: Total assets is the recorded value of all assets controlled by the business, including non-current and current assets.

items.prompt: State two points about employee numbers as a size measure: one use and one limitation. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Number of employees measures the size of the workforce. It is straightforward and useful for comparing labour use in similar businesses. Its limitation is that automation and differing part-time hours make headcounts less comparable. A highly mechanised producer can have fewer workers but far more output. Where hours differ, compare equivalent working time rather than ignoring the difference.
marking_guidance: Point: Number of employees measures the size of the workforce.

items.prompt: State two limitations of treating advanced machinery as proof that an enterprise is large. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Level of technology describes how advanced or extensive equipment and methods are. It can help explain productive capacity and why output is high with relatively few workers. Its limitation is that sophisticated equipment is a qualitative clue rather than a complete size measure: one advanced machine can belong to a small specialist. Underused technology need not produce large sales.
marking_guidance: Point: Level of technology describes how advanced or extensive equipment and methods are.

objective_titles: level of technology: Explain what this measure of business size captures and its limitation; do not substitute a generic definition unrelated to measurement.

items.prompt: State two points about market share as a size measure: one use and one limitation. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Market share is a business’s sales as a proportion of total sales in a defined market over a stated period. Use the same basis, such as sales value for both business and market. It indicates relative presence among competitors. Its limitation is that the market boundary matters: a large share of a tiny town market can represent fewer sales than a small share of a national market.
marking_guidance: Point: Market share is a business’s sales as a proportion of total sales in a defined market over a stated period.

objective_titles: market share: Explain what this measure of business size captures and its limitation; do not substitute a generic definition unrelated to measurement.

items.prompt: State two points about turnover as a size measure: one use and one limitation. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Turnover is sales revenue over a period. It indicates the monetary volume of sales and makes comparison of unlike products more useful than a physical unit count. Its limitation is that prices and the period covered affect it, and high revenue does not guarantee profit. A firm buying expensive goods for resale can have high turnover but a thin surplus after costs.
marking_guidance: Point: Turnover is sales revenue over a period.

objective_titles: turnover: Explain what this measure of business size captures and its limitation; do not substitute a generic definition unrelated to measurement.

items.prompt: State two distinctions between high profitability and a large scale of operations. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Profitability concerns the ability to generate profit relative to a relevant base such as sales or capital employed. It can help compare financial performance, but its limitation as a size indicator is that efficiency or a high margin is not the same as large operations. Absolute profit is the surplus after costs; a profitability ratio relates that surplus to another figure. Neither proves large employment or assets.
marking_guidance: Point: Profitability concerns the ability to generate profit relative to a relevant base such as sales or capital employed.
items.provenance: Original author prose derived from the named syllabus objectives; no official question text.
objective_titles: profitability: Explain what this measure of business size captures and its limitation; do not substitute a generic definition unrelated to measurement.

items.prompt: State two points about value of output as a size measure: one use and one limitation. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Value of output measures production in monetary terms over a period. It allows outputs of different kinds or sizes to be expressed on a common money basis. Its limitation is that changing prices and different valuation methods affect the result, and produced goods may remain unsold. Therefore value of output is not automatically the same as turnover, which relates to sales.
marking_guidance: Point: Value of output measures production in monetary terms over a period.

items.prompt: Explain why classification and consistent measurement help business decisions. A local planning office needs to assess employment opportunities in food processing. It receives employment totals for food factories and sales totals for farms. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Classification groups businesses by a shared characteristic, such as activity sector or ownership. Measurement indicates scale through an appropriate size indicator. Governments can use sector and employment information to identify where support or infrastructure may be needed. A lender can compare an applicant with businesses of similar activity and scale instead of interpreting its turnover without context. Managers can monitor changes over time and compare competitors. Investors may use size data as background, but size alone cannot establish return or safety. A classification is useful only if its categories fit the question. Primary/secondary/tertiary helps describe economic activity; public/private helps describe ownership. Neither directly ranks business size. Measurement must also be consistent: compare annual turnover over the same length of time and avoid comparing one firm’s sales revenue with another’s profit. Two businesses may be similar in employment but different in assets, so describe that result instead of forcing a single ranking. The purpose of the decision determines the most useful classification and measure. Food processing is secondary while farming is primary. The office should obtain comparable employment figures for the relevant processors before judging their job contribution. Farm turnover cannot be treated as the missing factory employee count.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Classification groups businesses by a shared characteristic, such as activity sector or ownership.

items.prompt: Explain how personal service and a niche market can help a small firm survive. Nela Stitch, a three-person workshop in Keetmanshoop, alters individual garments within a day. A large clothing outlet nearby sells standard sizes and does not offer alterations. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Small firms can survive by meeting needs that large suppliers cannot serve profitably or flexibly. A narrow local market may support a small repairer but not a large branch. Personal service can help an owner learn customer preferences, adjust an order quickly and win repeat business. A specialist may make customised goods that do not suit a standard production line. Close contact between owner, workers and customers can shorten decisions. Low overhead commitments may also help, although a small firm does not automatically have a lower cost per unit. Large rivals may obtain purchasing advantages if orders are sufficiently large and coordination remains effective. Small firms face disadvantages such as limited finance, dependence on a few customers and the owner’s limited time. Survival therefore requires enough demand and revenue to cover costs, not merely being friendly. Some owners deliberately remain small to preserve control and a manageable workload. Others are newly established businesses that may later grow. Judge survival against the actual customers and resources: a niche can protect a small supplier, but losing a major customer can make that niche too narrow. Nela serves a distinct tertiary service need with flexible personal attention. Customers needing a specific fit may pay for that convenience. Survival still depends on sufficient alteration orders to cover rent and wages; large retail sales nearby do not guarantee Nela’s demand.
marking_guidance: Starting point: Small firms can survive by meeting needs that large suppliers cannot serve profitably or flexibly.

items.prompt:
Fictional Nareta Repairs in Mariental employs four people and repairs customers’ bicycles. It buys replacement parts from a manufacturer. A large retailer nearby sells standard bicycles but offers no repairs. Nareta earns most of its revenue from individual repair jobs and can discuss each problem directly with its customer. Its owner is considering replacing that personal service with a much larger standard bicycle assembly operation. No firm order for assembled bicycles exists.

a(i) Define a primary-sector business. [2]
a(ii) State two reasons small firms may survive alongside large rivals. [2]
b State the activity sector of Nareta’s repair service and the activity sector of its parts manufacturer. [2]
c Explain two limitations of using employee numbers alone to compare Nareta with a highly automated parts manufacturer. [6]
d Evaluate whether Nareta should replace its personal repair service with large-scale assembly now. [8]
items.canonical_answer: a(i) A business that obtains natural resources, for example through farming or extraction. a(ii) Personal customer service and serving a specialist niche. b Repairs are tertiary; manufacturing replacement parts is secondary. c Automation allows the manufacturer to produce many parts with relatively few employees, so headcount understates its output compared with labour-intensive repairs. Employee count also omits investment in machinery: two firms could have the same workforce yet very different assets and productive capacity. Use employee numbers alongside turnover and asset or output measures for the same period. d Personal service meets a gap the retailer leaves and uses Nareta’s direct contact with each customer, supporting repeat repair demand. Larger assembly could increase output and could lower unit costs if sufficient standard orders use the capacity, but there are no firm orders and Nareta could lose its repair niche while committing to larger costs. Keep the repair focus now; reconsider expansion after testing demand, rather than treating size itself as the objective.

Review verified orders and capacity before growing; a larger premises count alone is not evidence of better performance.

Local households choose Omila for unusual sizes, and orders are sufficient for its present three-person operation. Omila could rent a bigger factory and concentrate on identical shades, but there is no firm demand for those extra units. For part (b) only, a guesthouse group now commits to a two-year order for identical shades sufficient to keep the proposed larger factory busy. All other facts are unchanged.

a Evaluate remaining small and customised under the original facts. Classify Omila’s activity and explain why one size measure alone is insufficient. [12]
b Evaluate the same choice after the stated guesthouse order arrives. Explain whether the original recommendation should change. [12]
items.canonical_answer: a Omila manufactures shades and is secondary. Three employees describe workforce size but omit productive equipment, sales and the high value of customised products. Its present demand fits a small operation; unusual sizes and personal attention distinguish it from the large standard supplier. Expanding might allow more output, yet the bigger factory would create commitments before demand is established. Remain small because the niche is proven for current scale whereas the standard market is not. This judgement would weaken if dependable standard orders emerged. b The two-year order changes demand certainty, not the fact that manufacturing is secondary. Expansion can now use the larger factory for a specified customer rather than speculative stock; standardisation may reduce unit costs if the order uses capacity efficiently and coordination is controlled. Against this, reliance on one guesthouse group creates risk at contract end and the larger operation could displace custom work. Shift towards the larger operation only after checking that the agreed order covers its extra commitments and can be delivered with the resources available. The recommendation becomes more favourable to expansion because dependable demand replaces the original uncertainty, while renewal and customer dependence remain reasons to limit longer commitments.
